To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) soluble amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptide can cross the blood-brain barrier and bind selectively in the brain to certain subtypes (subpopulations) of neurons, but not glia, 2) Abeta42 is found in brain parenchyma in Alzheimer's disease patients and 3) the blood-brain interface may serve as an important source of exogenous, blood-borne Abetapeptides that bind selectively to neurons in the brain.

(1) Abeta peptides cross a permeabilized BBB; (2) Abeta42 is found in the brain of AD patients, but not in control brains; (3) Abeta peptides bind selectively to neurons; (4) Abeta peptides can enter neurons; and (5) the BBB prevents the entry of Abeta peptides into a normal brain.

(i) blood-borne Ab42 peptides can cross a BBB rendered permeabilized by pertussis toxin and bind selectively to certain neuronal subsets in the brain; (ii) an intact BBB blocks the entry of blood-boned Ab42 into the brain; and (iii) blood-borne Aβ42 peptides bind to the same neuronal subsets as those that bind endogenous Ab42 peptides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that blood-borne, soluble Aβ peptides can enter and bind to neurons through a defective BBB.
the hypothesis that soluble Abeta peptides in the blood can bind selectively to neurons in the brain, and that these exogenous Abeta species may play a role in the pathophysiology of AD.
the role of the blood as a source of Abeta peptides that may enter the brain via a leaky blood–brain barrier (BBB).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the blood-brain barrier is not a significant barrier to Abeta42.
the blood-borne Aβ peptides can cross a permeable BBB and bind to certain neuronal sub-types in a subtype-specific manner.
blood-borne soluble amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides can cross the blood-brain barrier and bind selectively and differentially to neurons in the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
blood-borne Ab peptides can enter the CNS through a defective BBB and bind selectively to specific neurons, which may have implications for the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
blood-borne Aβ peptides can cross a permeable BBB and bind selectively to specific neuronal subtypes.
the BBB can be defective in AD and that blood-borne Ab peptides can enter the AD brain and interact with neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BBB is not an effective barrier against Abeta.
the BBB can become permeable to blood-borne Ab peptides, which can then bind selectively to certain neuronal cell types.
the brain has a unique vulnerability to exogenous Abeta, and this vulnerability is likely due to the unique properties of neurons, which are the main targets for Abeta.
